## General instructions

- The details of each DGP, including its numerical parameters and distributions, are intentionally unspecified.
  Choose them yourself, as you would in practice.
- Choose nonzero true values for all parameters evaluated using the 5% relative-error criterion.
- Grading criteria:
  - If an objective-function plot is not minimized near the true parameters when identification is expected, half of the points for that part will be deducted.
  - If an estimated parameter is not within 5% of its true value, half of the points for that part will be deducted.
- The input and output examples below are illustrative only.
- You may change them as needed to match your specification.
- The 5% relative-error criterion applies only to point estimates; for set estimates, verify that the true parameter lies in the estimated set.
:::

## The Idea of the Assignment

- This assignment asks you to conduct Monte Carlo experiments based on the
  following papers:
  - Martin Pesendorfer and Philipp Schmidt-Dengler (2008),
    [“Asymptotic Least Squares Estimators for Dynamic Games”](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-937X.2008.00496.x),
    *The Review of Economic Studies*, 75(3), 901–928.
  - Ying Fan and Chenyu Yang (2025),
    [“Estimating Discrete Games with Many Firms and Many Decisions: An Application to Merger and Product Variety”](https://doi.org/10.1086/734724),
    *Journal of Political Economy*, 133(6), 1886–1931.
- You will determine the model details yourself; only the basic framework is
  provided.
- You may simplify the specifications if needed.


## Question 1: Dynamic Discrete Game

### Summary

#### Setting

- Firms $i=1,\ldots,N$ play an infinite-horizon dynamic discrete game. In
  period $t$, firm $i$ observes the public state $x_t$ and private
  action-specific shocks $\varepsilon_{it}(a_i)$, then chooses
  $a_{it}\in\mathcal A_i$.
- Firm $i$'s period payoff is

  $$
  u_i(a_i,a_{-i},x;\theta,\varepsilon_i)
  =
  \pi_i(a_i,a_{-i},x;\theta)
  +
  \varepsilon_i(a_i).
  $$

- The public state follows the controlled transition probability

  $$
  G(x'\mid x,a),
  $$

  where $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_N)$.
- Let

  $$
  P_i(a_i\mid x)
  =
  \Pr(a_i\mid x)
  $$

  denote firm $i$'s conditional choice probability (CCP). Assume that the
  private shocks are independent Type-I extreme value random variables.

#### Equilibrium Condition

- Begin with a proposed collection of CCPs $P$. Average over the rivals'
  actions to obtain firm $i$'s expected current payoff from $a_i$:

  $$
  \bar\pi_i(a_i,x;P_{-i},\theta)
  =
  \sum_{a_{-i}}
  \pi_i(a_i,a_{-i},x;\theta)
  \prod_{j\ne i}P_j(a_j\mid x).
  $$

- The proposed CCPs also induce the public-state transition matrix

  $$
  F^P(x'\mid x)
  =
  \sum_a
  G(x'\mid x,a)
  \prod_jP_j(a_j\mid x).
  $$

- Up to an additive constant, the Type-I extreme value assumption gives the
  expected flow payoff under policy $P$ as

  $$
  r_i^P(x;\theta)
  =
  \sum_{a_i}
  P_i(a_i\mid x)
  \bar\pi_i(a_i,x;P_{-i},\theta)
  -
  \sum_{a_i}
  P_i(a_i\mid x)\log P_i(a_i\mid x).
  $$

- Evaluate policy $P$ by solving

  $$
  V_i^P
  =
  r_i^P+\beta F^PV_i^P,
  $$

  or equivalently,

  $$
  V_i^P
  =
  (I-\beta F^P)^{-1}r_i^P.
  $$

- To evaluate a one-period deviation to action $a_i$, hold firm $i$'s action
  fixed and integrate over the rivals' CCPs:

  $$
  F_i^P(x'\mid x,a_i)
  =
  \sum_{a_{-i}}
  G(x'\mid x,a_i,a_{-i})
  \prod_{j\ne i}P_j(a_j\mid x).
  $$

- The resulting choice-specific value is

  $$
  v_i^P(a_i,x;\theta)
  =
  \bar\pi_i(a_i,x;P_{-i},\theta)
  +
  \beta
  \sum_{x'}F_i^P(x'\mid x,a_i)V_i^P(x').
  $$

- The Type-I extreme value assumption gives the best-response CCP map

  $$
  \Psi_i(P;\theta)(a_i\mid x)
  =
  \frac{
  \exp\{v_i^P(a_i,x;\theta)\}
  }{
  \sum_{\widetilde a_i}
  \exp\{v_i^P(\widetilde a_i,x;\theta)\}
  }.
  $$

- A Markov-perfect equilibrium is a fixed point of this map:

  $$
  P=\Psi(P;\theta).
  $$

#### Estimation

- Estimate the CCPs from state-specific action frequencies in the simulated
  data:

  $$
  \widehat P_i(a_i\mid x)
  =
  \frac{
  \sum_{m,t}
  \mathbf 1\{a_{imt}=a_i,\ x_{mt}=x\}
  }{
  \sum_{m,t}
  \mathbf 1\{x_{mt}=x\}
  }.
  $$

- For each candidate $\theta$, keep $\widehat P$ fixed and repeat the policy
  evaluation above to compute $\Psi(\widehat P;\theta)$.
- Following the CCP minimum-distance approach in
  [Pesendorfer and Schmidt-Dengler (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-937X.2008.00496.x),
  define

  $$
  m(\theta)
  =
  \operatorname{vec}
  \left[
  \widehat P-\Psi(\widehat P;\theta)
  \right]
  $$

  and estimate

  $$
  \widehat\theta
  =
  \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta}
  m(\theta)'Wm(\theta).
  $$

- The optimization does not update $\widehat P$ or solve a new equilibrium at
  each candidate $\theta$.

## Question 2: Fan and Yang (2025)

### Summary

#### Setting

- Two firms $i\in\{1,2\}$ operate in market $m$ and simultaneously choose
  product portfolios.
- Each firm decides whether to offer each of $J$ products:

  $$
  a_{im}
  =
  (a_{i1m},\ldots,a_{iJm}),
  \qquad
  a_{ijm}\in\{0,1\}.
  $$

- Let $v_{jm}$ denote the known variable profit from product $j$, $C$ the
  common fixed cost, and $s_j$ an observed product exposure.
- Firm $i$'s payoff is

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  U_i(a_{im},a_{-i,m};C,\zeta_{im})
  ={}&
  \sum_j a_{ijm}(v_{jm}-C-\zeta_{ijm}) \\
  &-\eta\sum_{j<k}s_js_k a_{ijm}a_{ikm} \\
  &-\gamma\sum_j s_j^2a_{ijm}a_{-i,jm} \\
  &-\lambda\sum_{j\ne k}s_js_k a_{ijm}a_{-i,km}.
  \end{aligned}
  $$

- The second term captures cannibalization between a firm's own products.
- The third term captures competition in the same product.
- The fourth term captures competition across products.
- Treat $(v_{jm},s_j,\eta,\gamma,\lambda)$ as known, estimate $C$, and
  normalize

  $$
  \zeta_{ijm}\overset{iid}{\sim}N(0,1).
  $$

- This solution uses two firms and three products. Each firm has eight
  possible portfolios, and the market has $8^2=64$ action profiles.

#### The Idea

- Begin with a two-firm game in which each firm chooses one binary action,
  $a_i\in\{0,1\}$. The incremental payoff from action one is

  $$
  \Delta_i(a_{-i};\theta,\zeta_i)
  =
  d_i(a_{-i};\theta)-\zeta_i.
  $$

- Normalize the payoff shock as $\zeta_i\sim N(0,1)$.

- Suppose the actions are strategic substitutes:

  $$
  d_i(1;\theta)
  \leq
  d_i(0;\theta).
  $$

- If $\zeta_i<d_i(1;\theta)$, action one is profitable even when the rival
  chooses one. Action zero is then strictly dominated, so level-1 rationality
  requires firm $i$ to choose one. This gives the lower bound

  $$
  \Phi\!\left(d_i(1;\theta)\right)
  \leq
  \Pr(a_i=1).
  $$

- If $\zeta_i>d_i(0;\theta)$, action one is unprofitable even when the rival
  chooses zero. Action one is then strictly dominated and cannot be observed.
  This gives the upper bound

  $$
  \Pr(a_i=1)
  \leq
  \Phi\!\left(d_i(0;\theta)\right).
  $$

- The two-firm example therefore yields

  $$
  \Phi\!\left(d_i(1;\theta)\right)
  \leq
  \Pr(a_i=1)
  \leq
  \Phi\!\left(d_i(0;\theta)\right).
  $$

- These bounds use only the worst- and best-case incremental profits. The
  analyst does not need to solve the equilibrium or specify how an equilibrium
  is selected.
- In this assignment, each product decision $a_{ijm}$ plays the role of the
  binary action in the two-firm example. The firm's other product decisions
  and the rival's entire portfolio form the strategic environment.
- Holding those other decisions fixed, the incremental payoff from adding
  product $j$ is

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \delta_{ijm}(a_{i,-j,m},a_{-i,m};C)
  ={}&v_{jm}-C \\
  &-\eta s_j\sum_{k\ne j}s_ka_{ikm} \\
  &-\gamma s_j^2a_{-i,jm} \\
  &-\lambda s_j\sum_{k\ne j}s_ka_{-i,km}.
  \end{aligned}
  $$

- Because all interaction terms are strategic substitutes, setting all other
  relevant actions to zero gives the best case:

  $$
  \overline\delta_{jm}(C)=v_{jm}-C.
  $$

- Setting all other relevant actions to one gives the worst case. Define the
  resulting interaction penalty as

  $$
  D_j
  =
  (\eta+\lambda)s_j\sum_{k\ne j}s_k
  +\gamma s_j^2.
  $$

- Then

  $$
  \underline\delta_{jm}(C)
  =
  v_{jm}-C-D_j.
  $$

- Applying the same two-action argument product by product gives

  $$
  \Phi\!\left(v_{jm}-C-D_j\right)
  \leq
  \Pr(a_{ijm}=1\mid v_{jm},s_j)
  \leq
  \Phi\!\left(v_{jm}-C\right).
  $$

- The illustration has one action per firm, but the DGP below is a portfolio
  game. Product choices remain coupled even though the bounds are written for
  one product at a time.

#### Equilibrium Condition

- To generate data, this solution solves the small portfolio game directly.
- A pure-strategy Nash equilibrium is a pair of portfolios satisfying

  $$
  a_{im}
  \in
  \underset{a_i'\in\{0,1\}^J}{\arg\max}\;
  U_i(a_i',a_{-i,m};C,\zeta_{im})
  \qquad
  \text{for each firm }i.
  $$

- Each firm therefore compares its chosen portfolio with all eight possible
  portfolio deviations, not one product at a time.
- More than one portfolio profile may satisfy these conditions.
- The DGP selects uniformly from the pure-strategy equilibria only to produce
  observed actions. The estimator below does not use this selection rule.

#### Estimation

- Let $p_{jr}$ be the population probability that a firm offers product $j$
  in market type $r$.
- For a candidate $C$, define

  $$
  \ell_{jr}(C)
  =
  \Phi(v_{jr}-C-D_j),
  $$

  $$
  u_{jr}(C)
  =
  \Phi(v_{jr}-C).
  $$

- The population criterion is the largest violation of any probability
  inequality:

  $$
  Q(C)
  =
  \max_{j,r}
  \left\{
  [\ell_{jr}(C)-p_{jr}]_+,
  [p_{jr}-u_{jr}(C)]_+
  \right\}.
  $$

- The population identified set is

  $$
  \mathcal C_I
  =
  \{C:Q(C)=0\}.
  $$

- In the sample, aggregate choices to market-product offering shares, estimate
  $\widehat p_{jr}$ and its standard error $\widehat{se}_{jr}$, and calculate

  $$
  Q_M(C)
  =
  \max_{j,r}
  \left\{
  \left[
  \frac{\ell_{jr}(C)-\widehat p_{jr}}
       {\widehat{se}_{jr}}
  \right]_+,
  \left[
  \frac{\widehat p_{jr}-u_{jr}(C)}
       {\widehat{se}_{jr}}
  \right]_+
  \right\}.
  $$

- For an illustrative cutoff $c$, the sample acceptance set is

  $$
  \widehat{\mathcal C}_I
  =
  \{C:Q_M(C)\leq c\}.
  $$

::: {.callout-important}
## What changes when products interact?

- The DGP checks all 64 market profiles and all eight portfolio deviations for
  each firm.
- The Fan--Yang estimator evaluates only two one-dimensional normal CDF values
  for each product and market type.
- Product decisions are coupled through cannibalization and cross-product
  competition, but estimation does not require equilibrium computation.
:::
